title: A Good Narrow Cry
author: Marjory Teasel, midwife of Stillwater Landing
summary: An old river-port midwife sets down forty years at the bed-foot, from the loud births of her girlhood to the whispered ones of now.
text: I am asked by the girl who keeps the books at the Bonded Store, who can read and write and is not shy about either, to put down what I know before I am too old to know it. I said I had nothing in me worth the ink. She said then I could waste the ink, she would bring more. So this is her ink, and these are my hands, and you must forgive the both of them.

I have been the midwife at Stillwater Landing for forty-one years. I learned from my aunt, who learned from hers, and between us three women we have caught every child born on this basin since before the lock had iron gates. I have delivered the sons of every man who ever lied to the lockkeeper, and a fair few of the lockkeepers' own, and I will say no more about that, because they all still drink here.

When I was a girl a birth was a loud thing. I want that written down first, because the young ones do not believe it. A woman shouted if she liked, and she generally liked. The men stood in the yard and sang to keep from fretting, and if it went long they sang worse, and the whole wharf knew how a labour was going by the state of the singing. There was a reed hung over the birthing door, cut for the household by the Cantors upriver, and it sounded in every wind. And we waited for the first cry the way you wait for the tide to turn, with our whole bodies, and when it came we laughed out loud. I have heard a boatman cry at a first cry and not be ashamed of it. That was the world.

Then the Screaming Year came, and the hounds came with it, and by the next spring every birthing room on the Flume was packed with fleece and hung with felt like a coffin lined for winter. I cut my first bite-strap out of a harness my husband was still using. He noticed. I learned to put my mouth to a woman's ear and say, in the Narrow, love, in the Narrow, and to keep saying it, for hours if need be, until she could hear nothing else. I learned to measure a cry with my palm, a hand's width of voice and no more. I learned to be afraid of the very sound I had spent twenty years praying for.
You can learn anything. That is the dreadful thing about people.

I will tell one story from those years, because it is the one they ask for at the Store. Keziah off the rafts went into labour on a timber raft in the middle of the basin, with the drovers ashore and the lock shut and no boat to fetch her in. I rowed out alone with my bag on my knees. She had the strap in her teeth already and bit it so hard she broke a tooth on it, and she never once rose above a murmur, and I was prouder of her than of any woman I have ever tended. And then the boy came out roaring. A great red roar, the kind I used to laugh at, going out across the open water where there was no Hedge and no wool and nothing at all to stop it. Every soul on the wharf stood still. I could hear the reeds on the far bank go quiet, the way they do. And Keziah, without a word, took him off me and put him to the breast, and he stopped as if she had shut a door. There is no Narrow in the world as good as a full mouth. I have taught that to every girl since. It is the most useful thing I know.
Then they put the drill into the quarry at Oakhaven, and something came down the Flume that you could not see, and I learned to be afraid of the other thing.

I will not write much about the still ones. The Grafters call it infant pallor, and write it in their book, and go on to the next house. I am an old woman and I know what the old women call it, and I will not write that either, because some words you do not leave lying about where a child could pick them up. I will say only this. The first one I lost, I sat with the mother until the lamps were lit, and neither of us said anything, which was the worst thing we could have done and we both knew it. In the morning there was less of him. I have his name in my own book. I have eleven names in it now. I read them over on Nullday, under my breath, so that the room does not go quiet while I do.

It was a midwife upriver who put me right. She has no more voice than I have, a voice like a gate on a windy night, and she told me she had watched the Cantors hum through a clay jar laid to the belly, so that the note goes into the child instead of into the air, and that she did it herself when there was no Cantor to send for. I said I could not sing. She said the jar does not know that. She said a bad note held is better than a good note kept in your mouth, and she said it in a way that made me think she had lost a few before anyone told her, too.

So now I hum. I hum the Root note, low and flat and wandering, and I am sure it is the worst Root note ever sounded on this river. I hum it through the jar while the mother labours, and when the child comes out silent, which they do more often now, I bend over the soft of the head and hum it straight in. And mostly, not always, there is a breath, and a second, and then a small offended sound like a moth bumping a windowpane, and I say what my aunt said and her aunt before her, though the meaning has turned right round: there, a good cry. Only now I say a good Narrow cry. She'll live.

One thousand, eight hundred and six children, by my count, and by the girl's, who checked it. Most of Stillwater, then. If you are reading this at the Store, the odds are you were one of mine, and I have very likely smacked you since.

So here is my instruction, for what it cost me. Keep to the Narrow. Keep a lamp whistling. Keep a jar by the bed. And when your time comes, send for me, and if I am not there to come, hum anyway. Badly will do. Badly has always done.
notes: Canon used: Book One ch. 1 (the clay jar as a Cantor's trick for sending a note into a body; the Root note; felt on the door and fleece in the shutters; the bite-strap of boiled leather; "in the Narrow, love"; a sound "the width of a hand"; the still babies, which the Grafters call infant pallor while the old women call it what it is; the hush-lamp's reed). Series Bible Part IV, the Narrow (a screaming child calls the hounds, a silent one is a door left open); Part V (412 the Fracture and the Screaming Year; 417 the Oakhaven bore). Vol II, Reach (Stillwater Landing at the Flume's lower lock: a smugglers' town where timber goes out and Cantabile broadsheets come in); game text in js/flume16.js (Stillwater's wharf and basin). The unnamed upriver midwife with "a voice like a gate" is meant to be read as Bettany (Book One ch. 13 gives her "a voice like a saw in a knot" and shows her humming the tending note badly), but she is deliberately not named and nothing new is claimed about her. The Hush is shown only by aftermath. [PROPOSED]: Marjory Teasel and her life; her aunt who taught her; the raft birth (Keziah); the count of births; the girl from the Bonded Store who writes the book down; her husband and his harness.

title: Stone, Then Glass
author: Silas Hurlock, quarryman, of Oakhaven
summary: A quarryman who cut Oakhaven's millstones and chapel steps for thirty years tells, bluntly, what it is to work the same hole for the Consortium.
text: My name is Silas Hurlock. I have cut stone out of the Oakhaven quarry for thirty-four years, and for the last two I have cut none at all and been paid better for it, and I should like somebody to explain that to me before I die.

I went into the quarry at twelve, under old Master Cleeve, who had a voice like a dropped anvil and the softest hands in the Reach, because he had not used them for anything but pointing since before my father was born. In those days it was a hole in the ground and a good one. A bowl of grey stone, stepped down in terraces a quarter-mile across, and at the bottom of it the water, black and still, so cold in the summers that when you dived your teeth sang in your head. Half of Oakhaven learned to swim down there. I courted Meg on the third ledge with my boots off. She will tell you it was the fourth. It was the third.

The work was simple. You read the stone, you set your wedges along the line it wanted to break on, and you struck, and if you had read it right the block came away clean and rang when you tapped it, like a struck pot. That ringing was how you knew. A good block sang. A bad one thudded and you broke it up for rubble and said nothing about it in the alehouse. We cut millstones for every mill from here to Greenroot, and lintels for half the doors in town, and the steps of the Chapel of the Pure Note, which I will come back to.

In the year the Hedge went in, the Consortium came with paper from the Governor and pumped the bottom dry in eleven days. I stood on the rim and watched the water go down off the ledge where I courted Meg. Then they put the headframe in where the water had been, and since then the quarry has been lit from underneath, green as a bottle held up to a candle, all night and all day, so that you lose the habit of shadows.

I will tell you what the work is now, because nobody else will. We do not cut. We haul. We move timber for the shoring and iron for the gantries, we clear spoil off the terraces, we wheel barrows up and down the old steps I cut myself as a boy. We keep the glass-channels clean. We load the tanker-wagons at the bays and stand back while they go out east with a bell-headed soldier walking beside each one. Day-hands do not go down the shaft. I have never been down the shaft. I can feel it, though. Everyone can. It is in your back teeth from the moment you come through the gate, a grinding that does not stop, so that you go home at night and lie by your wife with your jaw aching like you have been chewing gravel. Meg says I grind my teeth in my sleep now. I tell her that is not me.

We are paid in scrip. Green and black paper with a drill and a wheel on it, which is to say a promise from the Consortium, signed by the Consortium, that the Consortium owes me. I am told this is money. The works store takes it at its face. The Boar & Dulcimer takes it too, and I will not say at what rate, because I have to go on drinking there.

Some things a quarryman learns. You do not stand near the soldiers at the gate. You pass them close because you must, and as you pass you hear what everyone hears, the murmur inside the bell, like somebody talking in their sleep in the next room. You learn to say good morning to them, very civil, because the Factor walks the line of them every morning with her coloured lenses on and listens to each one, and the young engineers say she can hear back everything they have seen. So I say good morning, and I say it nicely, and I have never once complained about the scrip within ten yards of a bell.

There is a crew at the pumps none of us has ever had a drink with. Contract men, the foreman says, brought in from elsewhere, who keep to the pumps the way the pumps keep to them. They do not come up to the canteen. They do not come up at all that I have seen. I asked once. The foreman looked at me the way Master Cleeve used to look at a block that thudded, and I have not asked since.

This year the bore-head went. I was on the third terrace with a barrow of spoil, and I felt it before I heard anything, a pitch climbing in my teeth like a kettle coming to the boil, faster than any kettle, and then the whole bowl jumped under me once, the way a dog jumps when you tread on its tail in its sleep. Then the green light down the shaft went brighter for a moment, and then quiet. They brought up four from the platform at the face. Marten, who owed me two Chimes from before the Fracture and knew it. Old Coyle. The Tanner twins, who were not twenty. The Cantor sang the twins down side by side, in the Narrow, so low that I had to stand near to hear it, and I stood near. The Consortium paid their mother in scrip.

Now the chapel steps. I cut them the summer I was twenty-two, eleven of them, out of the best seam the quarry ever gave. The third step from the top has a flaw in it shaped like a running hare. Master Cleeve wanted it broken up. I said nobody would ever see it but the people who looked at their feet, and those were the people I cut it for. He let me keep it in.

On Nulldays I go and sit on that step. It is the last stone in Oakhaven that does not glow, and does not hum, and does not ache in your teeth when you put your hand on it. It is just stone, cold, where I left it. Stone only ever wanted to be left where it was. You would think that was the easiest thing in the world to give it. Nobody did.
notes: Canon used: Book One ch. 5 (the quarry as a stepped bowl of grey stone a quarter-mile across, two hundred years old before the Consortium; millstones, chapel steps and lintels cut from it; children swimming in the flooded bottom, water cold enough to make the teeth sing; the headframe lit green-gold from below; cable-drums, tanker bays, glass-channels, gantries, depots, the mooring mast; the gatehouse clerk and the two Legionnaires at the gate; the Factor walking the Legion every morning with her lenses; the head that shattered and killed Marten, Old Coyle and the Tanner twins). Book One ch. 1 (the bore felt as an ache in the teeth; tanker-wagons going east daily with a Legionnaire beside each; the murmur inside the bell; the Root "being milked"; the Synod taking the bells for bore-teeth). Book One ch. 2 and ch. 4 (Consortium scrip, green and black, stamped with the drill-and-wheel). Book One ch. 1 (Lyra singing the Tanner twins into the ground). The pump-house men are a deliberate rumour; the author does not know who works the pumps (Book One ch. 5: Hollows), and the book does not say. CANON QUESTION: ch. 10 dates the deaths at the face to "the spring", while ch. 1 has Lyra burying the Tanner twins "at the end of summer"; the book avoids naming a season. [PROPOSED]: Silas Hurlock, his wife Meg, Master Cleeve the old quarry-master, the price of drink in scrip, the hare-shaped flaw in the chapel step.

title: The Pruner: A Life of Winifred Ruddock, Cantor of the Reed-Rows
author: Dorcas Lindley, of the Oakhaven dye-works, once her pupil
summary: An old dye-works woman remembers the Cantor who taught her for one year, tuned a valley with a pair of shears, and once sang a Church examiner into silence.
text: They will tell you a Cantor is a voice. Win Ruddock would have told you a Cantor is a pair of shears.

I was her pupil for one year, the year I was twelve, which was so long ago that the people who remember it with me could sit round one small table, and soon will not need to. I am writing this down because the young ones at the vats keep asking what the orchards were, and I find that I cannot tell them without telling them about her.

She was not a big woman. She was brown and narrow and bent a little forward, as if she were always walking into a wind, and she had the shears on a cord round her neck the way other women wear a locket. Every Cantor kept a row of the wind-reeds in those days, and Win kept the longest, the one that ran from the old stone wall clear down to the water, nine hundred reeds by her own count. A reed is tuned by cutting. Shorter sounds higher. Cut a hair too much and it is spoilt for a year. She would stand in her row in the evening with the wind coming down off the hills and listen with her head on one side, and then reach out, quick as a heron, and take the very tip off one reed out of nine hundred, and the whole row would come right. I never once saw her cut twice.

When the wind came properly, the rows sang. I do not know how to make you hear it. Slow chords, big as weather, rolling down the valley one into the next, so that a man ploughing at Greenroot would stop and lift his head. It was the most ordinary thing in the world, like rain. We did not even think it beautiful. You do not think your mother's voice is beautiful. It is just the sound the world makes when it is all right.

I came to her with no voice to speak of. My mother had hopes. Win heard me sing one verse of the harvest song and said, kindly, that I had a very good ear and a voice like a wet sack, and that ears were the rarer thing, and she would have me for a year anyway, because somebody had to hold the ladder. So I held the ladder. I carried the lantern and the twine and the pot of pitch for sealing cuts. And I watched her work, which no one else alive now did, and so it falls to me.

She sang to everything. To apple trees on frost nights, with her lips to the bark, a low note going down into the wood to keep the sap moving. To a farrier's boy in a fever, sitting on the end of his cot for two nights and never once raising her voice. To the cows at the Pellow place, which she said was nonsense but which made the farmer happy, and a happy farmer pays in cheese. She tuned the First Reeds for every child born in our end of the valley. She would lay a raw cane against the baby's breastbone and hum until the cane hummed back, and then cut the slot to what she heard, and that reed went over the door and sounded in every wind, and every Reed-Hanging after, the household cut the new one to the old one's note. My mother kept the first reed Win cut for me in a drawer for sixty years. I have it still. It still sounds.

She had sayings, and she said them so often that I can still hear the exact tune of them. One note is a shout, two notes is a conversation. Never sing to a tree you would not prune. A Cantor who wants to be listened to should go on the stage.
Now the thing everybody asks about, which is the man from the Church.

In the year I was with her, the Choir-Church sent an examiner up from the Organum to look into the Cantors of the Reach. Somebody had written to somebody that we taught the children intervals, which we did, and that intervals were the second note, which they are, and that the second note is sin, which every child in the Reach could recite and none of us believed. He came in white with a clerk behind him, a tall soft-spoken man who was polite to everyone and frightened Win's dog, and he sat in her kitchen and asked her to sing him one note, so that he could judge whether it was pure.

She said she would be glad to, but not indoors. She said a note wants room. She took him out into her row at dusk, and I came behind with the lantern, and she stood him in the middle of nine hundred reeds and opened her mouth and sang one note, the Root note, very plain, and held it.
And the wind came down off the hills.

I have thought about it for sixty years and I do not believe she planned it, and I do not believe she did not. The whole row took up her note and spread it into a chord, and the next row took the chord and turned it, and the next, all the way down the valley in the dark, until we stood in the middle of a sound as wide as the sky, with her one plain note still at the bottom of it like a stone at the bottom of a river. The examiner's clerk sat down on the ground. The examiner did not move at all. When it was over he stood there a long time. Then he thanked her, very civilly, and went back to the Organum, and I have been told by people who should know that his report on the Cantors of the Reach was two words long. Agricultural custom. We have lived inside those two words ever since. I like to think she wrote them.

She grew old the way the reeds did, from the top down. Toward the end she could not climb, and pruned from a stool that I carried behind her down the row, a few yards a day. She died in her chair by the window in the late summer of three hundred and ninety-one with the shears in her lap. We buried her at the bottom of her row, by the water, with her mouth free, as we did then. And the next spring her row came up out of tune for the first time in forty years, and nobody would touch it, and it stayed out of tune until the Cantors who came after her could bear to.

I was at the vats the morning the reeds went. I did not see it. By the time I got to the wall it was over, and the valley was full of something glittering, like frost blown off a roof, and the next gust took it away. People say there was a sound. I listened very hard, standing where I used to hold her ladder, and there was none.
It was the first thing in the Reach I ever heard go without a sound. I am glad, at least, that it was not her.
notes: Canon used: Book One ch. 1 (the wind-reed orchards planted in rows by the Cantors over three hundred years and tuned by pruning, singing chords heard from Greenroot; little wind-bells in the reed-rows; on the day the Spire broke every reed in the Reach turned in an hour to something like spun sugar and the next wind blew it to dust; tending notes for births, fevers and trees; the calling-song for lost lambs; the harvest song). Series Bible Part III (the catechism: holiness is one note, sin is the second note; the Church has suppressed the Cantors' craft for four centuries). Vol III A.1 (the Cantor craft as practical, agricultural, un-theological). Vol VII (b) §1 and §2 (the Synod tolerates the fields' customs as "agricultural custom"; Reed-Hanging and First Reeds tuned to each child's Signature). Game text js/sidequests.js (a reed tuned against a breastbone, the slot cut to what was heard). Book One ch. 6 and ch. 9 (the dye-works women as a body in the town). Burial before the Fracture is given without bound jaws or tongue-stone, which canon describes as a post-Fracture practice (Book One ch. 1). Tobin Ashgrove is deliberately not named or connected to Win. [PROPOSED]: Winifred Ruddock (c. 317 to 391 SR) and all her life; Dorcas Lindley; the Church examiner's visit and his report; the claim that "agricultural custom" began with his report is the author's belief, and she may be wrong.

title: Letters from the Gatehouse
author: Crispin Tolley, junior clerk to the Consortium of Bores, to his sister Prudence
summary: A young clerk from the Organum, posted to keep the ledger at the Oakhaven works gate, writes home to his sister about the Reach, the scrip, and the soldier who talks in its sleep.
text: Fair copies, kept, as a clerk should keep them.

Rootday the ninth of Seedmonth, 418. Dear Prue, I am here and alive and I have already disgraced myself. At the coaching inn at the edge of the Reach I asked the landlady, in an ordinary voice, whether there was any soup, and she put her hand flat over my mouth like a cork in a bottle and held it there until I stopped. Then she let go and said, very low, that there was. Nobody here speaks above a murmur. They measure their voices with the palm of the hand. Every room has a little lamp with a reed in it that whistles all night, so that the house is never quite silent, and the first night I lay awake listening to mine and thinking it was a kettle someone had forgotten. People greet you with "Does it ring?" and you are to say "True enough." I said "Yes, thank you," and was looked at.

My post is the works gate. I keep the ledger of every cart and wagon in and out, and pull the lever for anyone who holds up the green glass disc, and there are two soldiers of the Legion standing either side of me with their bells tilted to the sky. I miss the hour. Nobody plays it here. I did not know how much I leaned on it until I stood at a gate at what I am fairly sure was the sixth hour of the morning and had no idea whether it was.

Nullday the second of Lambmonth, 418. The soldier on the left of the gate talks in its sleep. They all murmur, you can hear it if you stand close, which you are told not to, but the one on the left says words. The same words, every morning, just before the day shift: second shelf, behind the flour. Second shelf, behind the flour. I am told this is nothing. There is a Catalogue circular pinned inside the gatehouse door which says that speech emitted by a damaged engram is to be disregarded and is not to be recorded. So I have not recorded it. I am telling you, which is different.

Dawnday the eleventh of Longsun, 418. You asked what the town is like. Prue, the fingernails grow. A quarter of an inch in a night. There is a knife beside every washbasin in Oakhaven and I have one by mine and I use it every morning before I shave. Little oaks come up through the cobbles overnight like teeth through a gum. When the wind gets up the big trees ring, actually ring, like spoons on a bowl, and everyone in the street stops and looks toward the Hedge. They took all the bells in the first year of the works, for the bore, and nobody here misses them, which is the strangest thing I have heard yet. At dusk the lamplighters go round, and old people take stools out to the crossings and hum till dawn. There is an old man at the Weavers' Cross who hums the same song every night and misses the same high note every time, and I have started walking home that way to hear him miss it. There is said to be a Synod man living alone outside the Hedge whom the hounds will not touch. Nobody will tell me his name, because I am from the Organum. I find I do not mind as much as I should.

Massday the third of Dustmonth, 418. Father writes that engrams are harmonic templates and possess no identity, and that I should not let rustic talk work on me. He is quite right. A template can hold a pattern of words the way a mould holds the shape of a loaf. The mould does not know it is a loaf. I have written that out twice to be sure I believe it. All the same I have begun to say good morning to the soldier on the left, because it seems rude not to, when one has heard about the flour every day for four months.

Memoryday the twenty-fifth of Firstfruit, 418. They have a rule here for children: never answer a voice you cannot see. Things outside the Hedge call in the voices of people they have heard. Last night at the Listening Hour I was walking the lane past the thorn and something on the other side said my name, quite kindly, in my landlady's voice. My landlady was in her kitchen. I could see her through the window, cutting bread. I did not answer. I walked on at the same pace, as they all do, and I was sick in the yard when I got in, and she held my head and did not ask. This morning I asked a woman at the well whether a voice inside a bell counts as a voice you cannot see. She looked at me for a long moment and then walked away without her water.

Nullday the twentieth of Stillmonth, 419. A hard winter, and the scrip will not change to sovereigns at anything like its face, so I am sending you less than I promised. I did a foolish thing. The Factor walks the line of the Legion every morning with her lenses, and listens to each soldier as if she were reading it, and this morning I asked her whether the one on the left of the gate might be posted somewhere else. I said it unsettled the carters. She looked at me through the coloured glass for a long time and said my colour was a little anxious, and that she would note it. Then she listened to the soldier on the left for longer than to any of the others. Prue, it occurs to me that if she can hear back everything it has heard, then she has heard me say good morning to it every day since Dustmonth. I do not know why that should frighten me. It is only good manners.

Rootday the seventh of Thawmonth, 419. I have stopped saying good morning. I am sorry to say I find I have begun to answer it instead, under my breath, the way you would answer anybody who told you the same thing every day. Behind the flour, yes. I know. I will look. I do not know what I would look for. I do not know whose flour. The circular says not to record it, and I have not, and I have been keeping the gate ledger very neatly.

Nullday the twelfth of Sheafmonth, 419. I have applied for a transfer home. Please do not tell Father until it is granted, and if it is not granted, please do not tell him at all. I am quite well. The harvest is coming in, and they have a festival here when the last field is cut, and I am told the clerk is not invited, which is fair. I only wanted to write down one more thing, and then I will not write about the gate again.

This morning, just before the day shift, the soldier on the left did not say anything about the flour. It said, quite clearly, in a voice like a little girl's, mind the step, Gran. There is no step at the gate. I minded it anyway.
Your loving brother, C.
notes: Canon used: Book One ch. 5 (the gatehouse clerk, the lever, the disc of green Root-glass as a pass, two Legionnaires either side of the gate with their bells tilted up; the Factor walks the Legion every morning with her lenses and can hear back what they have heard); the ch. 5 epigraph, Catalogue Circular 12, quoted exactly ("Speech emitted by a damaged engram is to be disregarded and is not to be recorded"); Book One ch. 1 (the Narrow, hush-lamps, the hand's width of voice, fingernails growing overnight and a knife by every washbasin, saplings in the cobbles, the oaks chiming, the bells taken for bore-teeth, night-hummers, old Tam at the Weavers' Cross missing the high note of "The Miller's Daughter", the man in the burner's hut who the hounds will not touch, the mimic rule); Book One ch. 2 (a Legionnaire murmuring about a blue jug: the murmur is ordinary Book One texture). Series Bible Book One cast (Factor Adela Vosk, who sees pitch as colour). Vol VI §3.1 (the Organum sounds the hour in one chord). Vol VII §5 (the Organum counts hours from the clock) and §6 (all weekdays checked by the formula). Vol II, Reach dialect ("Does it ring?" "True enough."). The clerk only suspects; what the cores are is never stated, and he argues himself out of it. [PROPOSED]: Crispin and Prudence Tolley and their father; the landlady; the Legionnaire's phrases; the clerk's exchange with the Factor (a small invented scene with a canon figure, kept to her known habits); his transfer request.

title: A True and Modest Account of the Life of Captain Teodor Brisk, Free Captain of the Air
author: Captain Teodor Brisk, written by himself, with a note by his bosun, Barnaby Gurney
summary: A Rust Coast captain who left the sea for the sky tells his own legend at full sail, and his bosun is given the last page to correct it.
text: I was born on the Rust Coast in a storm so famous that three separate taverns on the Long Mole claim it, and I have drunk free in all three on the strength of it. My mother said it was a squall. My mother was not a reliable witness; she was busy.

I signed the Articles at fourteen, like every man on this coast, and I could read them, which was rarer. I read them all the way through before I signed, and the old captain who held the pen laughed so hard he had to sit down. I tell young men this so they will know it can be done.

By twenty I had run the Roaring Strait eleven times by night with no lamp, steering by the pitch of the tide. Any child on the Coast can tell you what the sea is singing, but it takes a captain to hear when she is lying. I have been round Cape Dissonance in a gale with the coral howling under the keel like a choir that has been told bad news. I have wrestled an eel forty feet long in the shallows off the Cay with nothing but a boathook and my natural charm, and I have the scar. I have outrun a Synod frigate across open water in a coaster so slow that the gulls used to land on her to rest. I have dined with the Harbour-Queen herself, at her own table, and she laughed at my stories, and she does not laugh at many.
I have never once been afraid. I mention it only because people ask.

In the year after the Fracture the sea became unreliable in its manners. You will know what I mean if you are from the Coast, and if you are not, I will tell you plainly. The tides began to sing in keys nobody had charted. Water forgot what it was, here and there, and went soft and blue and thick as jelly, and a good hull would settle into it at her moorings like a spoon into custard. Holes opened in the sea. Not storms. Holes. I watched a coaster go down into one off the Cape with all her sails set, and the water closed over her afterward without a ripple, and there was no sound from it at all.
I am not a fool. I sold my hull while she was still a hull, and I bought a ship that does not touch the water.

She is the Fair Excuse. Ninety feet of patched grey envelope, a gondola built by a man who drank, and four lift-tanks under the keel that burn blue at night and hum like a congregation that has forgotten the words. On a still night you can hear her coming two miles off. She sounds like a barn being dragged across the sky by somebody who loves it. I have flown her from the Coast to the Reach and back more times than I have counted, and I have carried anything you care to name. Black glass. Rum. Salt mutton. Cheese, which is worse than glass for the smell. A bishop, once, who was sick on my boots and blessed them after.

I have never carried the bottles. I want that printed, and printed large. The Coast sells the last words of the dead in stoppered blue glass to anyone who is grieving and has money, and when the grieving pull the stopper the hounds come to the sound. I will not have them aboard. I have no wish to meet a hound at four hundred feet with nowhere to step back to. If you want to hear your dead husband say goodbye, get somebody else to fly it to you, and stand well away when you open it.

I hold to the Articles. All of them, but the First above the rest: no captain shall leave a hand in the water while the ship can bear the weight. The Harbour-Queen amended it in her own hand three years ago, as every captain knows, with the words or until she cannot. I am told that amendment was needed. I have never had cause to use it, and I never shall.

That is my life so far, and I commend it to the young as an example of what courage and modesty can do with very little money. I have been asked to let my bosun write a page at the end, for balance. I said he could have a short one.
A note by Barnaby Gurney, bosun of the Fair Excuse.

The eel was a conger and about four feet long and it bit him, and that is the scar. The frigate was a customs cutter and it caught us, and he talked us out of it, which is the cleverer thing and he will not tell it. The Harbour-Queen has asked the printer to set down that she has never dined with Captain Brisk, has never laughed at him, and is owed eleven sovereigns by him, payable at the Mole office.
He says he has never been afraid. He sleeps with a lamp lit and the hatch open every night of his life, so that he can hear the ship breathing. Make of that what you like.

But the part about the Article is true, and it is the only part I would have you remember. There are nineteen of us aboard a ship built to carry nine. We have a cook who cannot hear and a rigger with one hand and a lookout who cannot see past his own nose and listens instead. We have two old women who were hands on his first coaster and are no use to anybody, and a boy who was crying on the Mole one morning and has never been asked where he came from. Every captain on this coast has told him to put us ashore. He has never put one of us ashore. He says the ship can bear the weight.
That is why she flies so low.
notes: Canon used: Book Two Part One ch. 1 to 7 (the Articles of the Free Captains, which every man on the coast signs at fourteen; Article the First, "No captain shall leave a hand in the water while the ship can bear the weight", and its amendment in the Harbour-Queen's hand dated the eleventh of Frostmonth 414, "or until she cannot"; Port Cantabile on singing coral whose note tells the tide; a sovereign a pellet for glass shot; the Lantern Yard). Series Bible Part IV and VI (vox-bottles, the last words of the dead, bring hounds when opened; tonal trenches open in the sea like mouths; water forgetting its surface tension and turning to blue jelly; the Roaring Strait and Cape Dissonance; Oona Salt as Harbour-Queen). Book One ch. 14 and 21, Book Two (skyships: a patched envelope, lift-tanks humming and burning cobalt, the sound of "a barn being dragged across the sky"). Vol I and II (Broadsheet Row as the only free press; the Archipelago greeting "What's she singing?"). Nothing is said or implied about Vane or the Drift-Kestrel; the amendment is mentioned only as a line of law. The Harbour-Queen's printed denial is the only new act given to a canon figure, and it is a one-line notice. [PROPOSED]: Captain Teodor Brisk, the Fair Excuse and her crew, Barnaby Gurney, the eel, the customs cutter, the eleven sovereigns.

title: A Year of Nights
author: Godwin Pettigrew, lamplighter of Oakhaven
summary: An Oakhaven lamplighter keeps a year's notes on his round of whistling lamps, the people who sit up with them, and one night-hummer in particular.
text: Sheaf on the gate, 418. My mother kept a book of the weather and my father kept a book of debts, and I have neither weather nor money worth the writing, so I shall keep a book of nights. I light two hundred and twelve hush-lamps, from the tannery steps to the top of Cooper's Row, with a pole, a taper and a bad knee. People think a lamplighter's trade is fire. It is not. Any fool can light a wick. A lamplighter's trade is listening. When the flame takes, the reed in the chimney catches the draught and begins to whistle, and every reed has its own note, and I know all two hundred and twelve the way a shepherd knows his ewes. If one is wrong I hear it from the end of the lane.

Last lamp of the round is the one at the corner by the well, which I call Well Corner because nobody else has bothered to call it anything. Tibby Lockwood sits up there. She is a night-hummer, and younger than most of them, being only my age, and she hums lower than anyone in Oakhaven. You have to stand quite close to be sure she is humming at all. I stand quite close. It is my job.

First frost. Oil is four pence the pint and the Consortium says it will be five by the thaw. I said this to Tibby, who said nothing, because she was humming, which is the trouble with courting a night-hummer. I did not say I was courting. I am writing it here so it is written somewhere.

Frost again, harder. The lamp at the end house by the dye-works went wrong in the night. The cold split the reed, and it stopped whistling, and I was at the far end of the Hollow and did not hear it go. In the morning the door was on the latch. Her kettle was cold on the hob. Her shawl was on the back of her chair, folded the way she folded it, and there was nobody in either. Her name was Abigail Starling. She was seventy, and deaf in one ear, and she liked her lamp turned low so it would not keep her up. I have written her name here so that it is written somewhere too. I carry six spare reeds in my coat now, wrapped in flannel against the frost, and I walk the round twice.

Snow on the Hedge. Nails. I cut mine every morning by the basin with the little knife, the same as everyone, and this morning I cut them twice, because I lit the round late and lay in. Tibby says a man can tell how long he has slept by his fingers now, like a tree. That is the most she has said to me in a month. I am counting it.

Ice off the Flume. Walking home past the thorn at the dead hour I heard my mother call my name from the other side of it. Godwin, your supper is going cold. She has been dead four winters. She used to say it at the door every night of my boyhood, in exactly that voice, a little cross, a little fond. I made the sign, two fingers to the lips and to the ear, and kept walking at the same pace, which is the hardest thing I have ever done with my legs. When I got to Well Corner I must have looked a sight, because Tibby stopped humming and took my hand and held it, and then began again, and did not let go until the hummers changed.

Seed in. At the change of the hummers the old ones murmur all's well, all's quiet, keep to the Narrow, as they hand over the stools, and I have taken to saying it with them under my breath, though I am not one. Old Tam at the Weavers' Cross hums The Miller's Daughter every night of his life and every night he goes for the high note at the end of the verse and misses it. I said to Tibby that one of these nights he would get it. She said she hoped not. She said if Tam ever got that note it would be because something was out there listening hard enough to make him try. I have not been able to get that out of my head.

Reeds hung. The whole street was noisy all day with the tuning of the new First Reeds over the doors, and the Chapel sent a deacon round to say it was a very great deal of second notes for one street, and everyone said yes, deacon, and went on tuning. I looked at the reed over Tibby's door when I passed. Her mother still cuts the new one every year and tunes it against Tibby's breastbone at the kitchen table, as if she might have changed. She never has. It is a good low reed. I would know it anywhere now.

Hay in. I have done something I shall probably have to confess. I cut a new reed for the hush-lamp at Well Corner. I tuned it at home at the kitchen table for nine nights, against the lamp across the lane, which is my own lamp, the one on my own house. I tuned it a third above. The Church teaches that holiness is one note held without end, and that the second note is sin, and I was raised to say it and I said it. But I have listened to two hundred and twelve reeds a night for eleven years, and I tell you every one of them is lonely.

Eels down the Flume. The Eel-Run, late this year, because everything is late. The lamplighters set out the lanterns all down the bank for the fishing, and then the whole town stood along the water in the dark with traps and lines and nobody spoke at all, because the eels can hear. It is the only festival in the Reach you keep with your mouth shut. Tibby fished beside me for three hours without a word, which I found I liked very much. At the end she put an eel in my bucket, a fat one, and went home. In the Reach that is very nearly a proposal. I am almost sure.
Corn standing. They say at the well that the Church has views about the Last Sheaf this year. Let them have views. The north field will still be standing when they are gone.

Tonight I put the new reed in the lamp at Well Corner. I lit it last, as always, and the reed caught and whistled, and across the lane my own lamp answered it a third below, and the corner by the well made a chord. Very small. No louder than two people breathing in the same room. Tibby came up the lane with her stool and her shawl and stopped dead and listened to it for a long time, with her face doing nothing at all. Then she sat down, and settled her shawl, and began to hum.
She hummed the low note. Under both of them.
notes: Canon used: Book One ch. 1 (lamplighters with poles and tapers lighting the hush-lamps at dusk, each reed beginning to whistle as it catches; night-hummers with stools and shawls at the crossings; the change at the dead hour, "all's well, all's quiet, keep to the Narrow"; old Tam at the Weavers' Cross humming "The Miller's Daughter" and missing the high notes; the ward-sign, two fingers to the lips and then the ear; the mimic rule; fingernails and the knife by the basin; saplings in the cobbles; the corner by the well; the Chapel of the Pure Note; the Hollow behind the tannery; Cooper's Row). Book One ch. 6 (Tam never reached the high note in eighty-one years; the dye-works women; one of them takes his stool afterwards). Series Bible Part III (the second note is sin) and Part IV (a person who falls truly silent in siphoned country begins to unwrite). Vol VII (b) §2 (the Reach dates by what is growing; the Last Sheaf hung on the Hedge-gate; Reed-Hanging; the Eel-Run kept in near silence with lanterns along the Flume; moot-curd). Review of the Moor serial, finding 7 (lamp-oil at four pence the pint). The Hush appears only as an empty chair. The book ends before Book One opens. Entries are headed by what is growing, as a Reach man would date them. [PROPOSED]: Godwin Pettigrew, Tibby Lockwood, Abigail Starling, the round of two hundred and twelve lamps, Well Corner as a name for the crossing by the well, the retuned reed.

title: The Reeds-Miner: A Short Life of Tomas, Timber-Cutter, Against His Wishes
author: Hazel Fitch, his sister's daughter, for the Timber Compact's harvest supper
summary: A niece writes, for the timber-cutters' supper, the life of the uncle who told her not to: how a man who dug reeds for the Cantors came to fell ringing oaks for the Synod.
text: My uncle Tomas does not want this written. He said so, at length, across his own kitchen table, with the glove off so that I would have to look at the hand while he said it. I am writing it anyway, because the Compact asked me to, and because I am the only one in the family he cannot frighten, having been sick on him as a baby.

You will all have wondered why he is called the Reeds-Miner, when he has cut timber the whole of your acquaintance. Here is the answer. Before the Fracture, when a wind-reed went sour in the orchards, the Cantors could not simply pull it out. The crown sat a yard down, a knot of root the size of a man's head, and if you left any of it the new reed came up out of tune. So there was a trade for lifting them, with a long narrow spade and a lantern, and the men who did it were called reeds-miners, because they went down a hole in the ground and came up dirty. My grandfather did it. Tomas went down his first hole at eight, because he was the only one small enough. He could tell a sour crown by the smell before he touched it. The Cantors trusted him. He says that was the best thing anyone ever paid him in.

On the day the Spire broke, all the reeds in the Reach went to sugar and blew away in an hour, and his trade went with them. He was thirty-three and had a wife and a spade. Within the month he had a timber licence from the Synod and a grey mare called Dumpling, who is still with us, and still bites.

He was a good timber-cutter and a very loud one. In those days a wagon creaked. Everything creaked, and you could hear him coming down the Greenroot road from a mile off, singing to the mare, badly, in a voice that the Compact men tell me could split a log by itself.

Then the Consortium put the bore into the quarry, and the oaks began to ring like bronze when the wind moved them, and the wagons stopped creaking and began to hum, and the hounds learned that a ringing tree is a dinner bell. Tomas stopped singing. He learned to fell a bough with wool wound on the blade, and to wait for a gust to cover a stroke, and to call the work off when a hound lifts its head, with two notes, falling, which my aunt says is the only tune he has ever got right.

Last year the saw took three fingers off his hand. The fourth grew back, as things grow back here now, and it grew back wrong, and that is all I will say about the glove, because he will read this. He went back to the clearing nine days later. He says he has one good hand and a bad temper and that people may choose which they speak to. Most choose the hand.

He works for the Synod's quota, as some of you do. If he is a load short on quota day they take the wagon and Dumpling, and then he has nothing. So he fells what he is told to, a stone's throw from where the hounds sleep, and carts it up to the works, where it goes to shore the headframe over the shaft. He told me this himself. He said, I know what it holds up. He said he has been thinking it since the summer. I did not ask him what he thinks, because I could see.
At the end of the evening I asked him what he would like written, since it was going to be written whether he liked it or not.
He was quiet for a long time. Then he put the glove back on and said, write that the wagons used to creak.
notes: Canon used (game text, js/sidequests.js, the Tomas quest): Reeds-Miner Tomas, timber-cutter, works the clearing; "Does it ring? True enough"; the wagons do not creak any more, they hum, and "a man could miss a creak"; "I have one good hand and a bad temper"; three fingers to a saw and the fourth grew back wrong, kept in a glove; the Synod's quota day, and the Synod takes the wagon and the mare if he is short; iron-boughs ring like a bell when struck and a hound comes to a ring; he calls a felling off with two falling notes; the timber goes to shore the headframe, "I know what it holds up", and he has been thinking about it since the summer. Vol II, Reach (Tomas as a canon NPC; the Timber Compacts as the Reach's timber labour). Book One ch. 1 (the oaks began to ring after the bore went into the quarry; the wind-reeds turned to sugar-glass in an hour on the day of the Fracture). Growth law-rot (Series Bible Part IV) is why the finger grew back. [PROPOSED]: what the title Reeds-Miner means (lifting dead wind-reed crowns for replanting), his father's trade, his age, his wife, the mare's name, the date of the saw accident (418), Hazel Fitch, the harvest supper. These are new facts about a minor canon figure and can be cut without touching the quest.

title: A Shepherd's Ear: Letters from the Conservatory of Bores
author: Rafe Hatherly, scholar of the Conservatory, to his mother at Wethercombe
summary: A shepherd's son from the Downs wins a place at the Synod's great school for drill-engineers and writes home about forks, ewes and the city that plays the hour.
text: Nullday the fourth of Sheafmonth, 414. Dear Mam, I am here and I have not been robbed, though a man in the coach-yard tried to sell me a map of the city for two pence and the city is mostly straight lines, so I suppose I was nearly robbed. You will want to know what it is like. It is like standing inside an organ, if the organ were a mile wide and somebody had laid the streets between the pipes. The towers are grey and very tall and have mouths cut near the top, and the wind blows across them all day so that the whole city breathes one long low note you feel in your teeth. Then on the hour the bellows under the Choir-Hall push, and every pipe sounds at once, and the hour comes down on you like weather. The first time, I sat down in the road. Nobody laughed. A woman with a basket said I would stop hearing it in a week, and walked round me.

I lodge over a cordwainer's in a room with a window and a bed and a smell of leather. There are forty of us in the first year. I am the only one from the Reach. There is a book on every desk with a name on the spine from our end of the world, and you know whose, and I shall not write it, and you will not say it at the Bellwether, and that will be best for both of us.

Stasisday the twentieth of Ashfall, 414. Our first lesson was one line, and we spent a week on it. A struck fork held near a second fork a little out of true will beat. Loud, soft, loud, soft. Mam, I knew that before I came. It is the two bells on Father's old wethers on the far side of Hob's Knap, one a hair flatter than the other, so that you could hear them pulsing together across the whole down on a still evening, and tell from the beat which way the flock was moving. I said so in class. Everyone laughed except Master Hollister, who said that I had a shepherd's ear, and that a shepherd's ear was worth more in this building than the Synod's money, and then gave me twice the work.

Memoryday the first of Frostmonth, 414. The woman with the basket was right. On the eighth day I stopped hearing the hour. I know it still sounds, because I see the others look up at it, and I can feel it in the floor of my room if I put my hand there. But my ears have let it go. Brann, who sits next to me and is from the Peaks and says almost nothing, says that is how you know you have become a citizen. How many lambs did we lose in the cold snap? Tell me the true number, not the one you think I can bear.

Rootday the ninth of Seedmonth, 415. I have been spoken to. Brann and I were checking a pair of forks in the practice room, and to save time I hummed the one and he hummed a fifth above it, the way the old Cantors used to, so we could hear if the forks sat true between our notes. Master Hollister came in and stood there until we stopped. He was not angry. He said that we must not do that, that it was a folk habit, and that in this building it was very nearly devotional, in the wrong direction. Then he checked the forks himself, with a little brass meter, and they were true, and he said nothing more about it. Brann has not hummed since. I find I hum all the time now, under my breath, in my room, so the room is not so quiet. It is the Root note. I do not think I could stop if I tried.

Massday the third of Dustmonth, 415. Second year. Today we began the anatomy of the voice. There was a sheep's larynx on a tray at the front of the room, and the lecturer turned it with a probe to show us the folds and where they lie, and how they are stretched to change the note. Mam, it was a Downs ewe. I would know that gristle anywhere, I have helped Father with enough of them. I did not say so this time. I have learned that much. Nobody has told us why men who drill rock must know exactly how a voice is made, and where a wire would sit along it. When Brann asked, the lecturer said we would understand in our fourth year. Brann wrote it in his book. I wrote it in mine.

Memoryday the twenty-seventh of Sheafmonth, 415. We drilled our first sample in the works yard, a block of lively stone from somewhere east, set in an iron cradle with a little bore-head no bigger than a churn. We were to hold the bit beneath the failure-pitch, as the book on every desk says we must, always beneath. I had the meter. And as the bit went in, the stone's pitch climbed away from it, a little, the way a ewe shifts away from the shears when she feels the first cold of the blade. Master Hollister said samples are lively and that we would learn to correct for it. Tarquin, who is from the Organum and very clever, asked whether stone could mind. Everyone laughed. He was not in the hall at the start of term. They said his family had sent for him.
Nullday the eighteenth of Lambmonth, 416. Dear Mam, I am coming home.

I have not failed. Master Hollister says I am the best ear in the year and he wrote it down and I will bring you the paper so you can show it at the Bellwether, which I know you will. I have not been sent away. I have done something worse, which is to leave a scholarship, and Father would have had a great deal to say about it, and I will listen to all of it from you instead.

I will tell you the reason, because you will ask, and because I have only just found it out myself. This morning I walked across Registry Square at the hour, and the whole city sounded, every pipe, and I did not hear it. Not at all. A year and a half I have not heard it. And I thought: they told me I would stop hearing it, and they were pleased when I did, and so was I. And then I thought about the stone in the yard, shifting away from the bit, and the ewe on the tray, and Tarquin, and I understood that I am being taught, very carefully and very well, to stop hearing things.
So I am coming home by the Reach road and I will be at the stile before Reed-Hanging. Please do not take my reed down. I should like to hear it.
notes: Canon used: Series Bible Part VIII (the Conservatory of Bores at the Organum; Kaelen entered at seventeen on a scholarship the town was proud of). Book One ch. 15 (Conservatory course 402 to 406, four years). Book One ch. 5 (Kaelen's book "On the Calibration of Resonant Bores", printed 409, studied by students; "hold beneath the failure-pitch"). Book One ch. 2 (he was told he had the finest ear for failure in forty years). Book One ch. 10 (the anatomy of the voice taught in the second year, in a room with a sheep's larynx on a tray). Book Two Part Two (the first line of the first revision of the Vance Sequence: "A struck fork held near a second fork a little out of true will beat", written to explain to first-year students why no two bore-heads draw the same). Vol VI §3.1 (the Organum's towers are pipes; the city sounds the hour in one chord audible thirty miles out; everyone stops hearing it within a week, and that is the point). Series Bible Part III (the second note is sin). Vol VII (b) §2 (Reed-Hanging and First Reeds). Phase 20-21 Author Rulings and js/sheepwalk22.js (Wethercombe, the Bellwether, the Downs flocks, later shorn for the Hedge's wool in 417 and eaten in the shut years: the letters predate this, and a reader in 419 knows there are no sheep). Kaelen is never named; the boy only knows the name on the book. Why engineers learn the voice is left unanswered. [PROPOSED]: Rafe Hatherly and his mother, the lodging over the cordwainer's, Brann from the Peaks, Master Hollister, the test sample in the works yard, the student who left.

title: Between the Falls
author: Marthe Unhaus, of Tier Eleven, for the Bellows
origin: Broadsheet Row, Port Cantabile, from a copy carried out of Cinderhold
summary: A woman from the lowest, hottest tier of Cinderhold tells how four hundred workers with no House learned to organise in the gaps between the hammer-blows.
text: Set on the Row from a copy carried out of the Caldera in the lining of a boot. The Bellows do not sign their papers. We print the name she gave us, which is not a name, and you will see why.
Still standing.

That is how we say good morning on Tier Eleven, and it is not a joke, though you may laugh. I was born at the bottom of Cinderhold, where it is hot enough that a heel of bread goes to rusk in your pocket between the gate and the furnace. Tier One has clean air and a House. Every tier below it has a House, all the way down, until you come to us, and we have none. So we are written down in the indenture books as Unhaus, of no house, and some of us have taken it for a surname out of spite. I am one. You are born owing on Tier Eleven, for your mother's bed and the water she drank while she carried you, and you work it off, and you die owing more.

Above everything is the Beat. If you have never heard the Great Beat I cannot give it to you, any more than I could give you the heat. It is a hammer the size of a chapel, and it falls in fours, and it has fallen in fours for two hundred years except on two days that we count our history from. You do not hear it after a while. You live in it. A child on Tier Eleven learns to talk in the gaps, between one fall and the next, three counts of speech and then shut your mouth, because on the fall nobody hears anything, not even the person shouting. Outsiders talk across the fall and you see their lips going and you feel sorry for them. I have been told that when we go abroad we stop in the middle of sentences for the rest of our lives. I have never been abroad. I expect it is true.

My father kept his hand on it. That is the best thing you can say of a man in Cinderhold. When an oath is sworn among us it is sworn bare-handed on an ingot just out of the mould, and the one swearing holds his palm there while the oath is said, and a man who takes it off before the end is cold, and there is no worse word. My father took the Bellows' oath with his hand on the ingot for the whole of it. He had the mark till he died. He died cold anyway, not that way, the other way. The Cold Burn went through our furnace the winter I was twelve and the heat went out of him with it. He walked about for a year with his eyes open and no warmth in his hands, one of the ember-blind, and I used to hold them to warm them, and it was like holding two spoons.
We are called the Bellows because a bellows is the only part of a forge that breathes, and nobody has ever thanked one.

There are four hundred of us. We have no leverage, as the Houses are fond of telling us, and no money, and no hall. What we have is the Beat. A meeting of the Bellows is held in the open, in the noise, because no overseer can hear a thing in it. Questions are put between the falls. We vote by tapping the pipe-rail, once for aye and nothing for nay, in the gap after the fall, and a man down the line counts, and four hundred people can decide a thing in the time it takes the hammer to fall eighty times. I have stood in a vote like that with my brother Hanno on one side and a girl I had never met on the other, and felt the rail ring under my palm with four hundred taps, and I will tell you it is the nearest I have come to hearing a choir.

In the spring of four hundred and fifteen we sat down. Three days, every hand on the tier, sitting on the walkways with our arms folded. The Houses brought in slag-folk from the Scraps, who have even less than we do and could not be blamed, and paid them in food, and the furnaces never once went out. On the fourth day we stood up and went back owing more. Hanno says that is how we learned the first law of Cinderhold, which is that nothing done here is louder than the Beat. He says it as if it were the end of something. I think it was the beginning.

I will put down one more thing, because the Row asked for it. Men who come up from the deep galleries say that the glass down there talks. I do not mean it rings. I mean talks. They do not say this above Tier Nine. Below it they say it all the time, very quietly, between the falls, and they say it the way you would mention that a neighbour has been crying in the night, and that someone should go round.

Upstairs the Houses have started calling something the Gasket Strike. They have given it a name before we have, which is how we know they are frightened, because you only name the thing you are expecting.
We have learned to say everything that matters in the space between two blows of a hammer. It has always been room enough. One day the hammer will have to wait for us.
Still standing.
notes: Canon used: Series Bible Part VI and VII (Cinderhold, the forge-spire of steam hammers; the Cold Burn, fire that freezes and frost that scalds; the ember-blind, whose inner heat has gone out; the Deep Guilds, worked to death by the Consortium, who have heard the deep seams whisper; the Gasket Strike brewing). Vol II, Cinderhold (eleven tiers, Tier Eleven the hottest, indentured, with no House; the Great Beat, which has stopped twice in two hundred years; the Bellows as Tier Eleven's unrecognised union, four hundred members, no leverage, extraordinary courage; Slag-Town Scraps on the tailings; dialect "Still standing", "On the ingot", "cold" for cowardly, "he kept his hand on it" from the bare-handed ingot oath; Cinderholders pausing in rhythm for life). js/books.js (the Great Beat keeps four counts; people speak between the falls). Vol I and II (Broadsheet Row as the only free press; broadsheets reach the Reach through Stillwater). The deep seams' whisper is told only as a rumour that is not spoken above a certain tier; nothing is said of what the glass is made of. [PROPOSED]: Marthe Unhaus, the surname Unhaus taken by people of no House, her father and brother Hanno, the pipe-tap vote, the failed sit-down of 415, the printer's preface.
